entries.e5f35220f7364c77a01a4b6a675da6c5f3b0527d: <div sID="gen32551" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="2Tim.4" sID="2Tim.4"/> <div eID="gen32551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32552" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32553" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, I. Paul with great solemnity and earnestness presses Timothy to the diligent and conscientious discharge of his work and office as an evangelist; and the charge given to him all gospel ministers are to take to themselves, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.1-2Tim.4.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. The reason of his concern in this case, Why must Timothy now be instant in season, &c., in a particular manner? Because the church was likely to be deprived of the apostle's labours, for his departure was at hand, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.6-2Tim.4.8">ver. 6-8</reference>. III. Divers particular matters, with a hint and caution, about Alexander the coppersmith, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.9-2Tim.4.15">ver. 9-15</reference>. IV. He informs him of what befel him at his first answer; though men forsook him, the Lord stood by him, and this encouraged him to hope for future deliverance (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.16-2Tim.4.18">ver. 16-18</reference>) And then he concludes with salutations and a benediction, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.19-2Tim.4.22">ver. 19, to the end</reference>.
entries.fa098b9e6f1a7d4a198331213f919fc411128910: <div eID="gen32553" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32552" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Ministerial Duties; The Apostle's Joyful Expectation. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen32554" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> I charge <hi type="italic">thee</hi> therefore before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, who shall judge the quick and the dead at his appearing and his kingdom; <hi type="super">2</hi> Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine. <hi type="super">3</hi> For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears; <hi type="super">4</hi> And they shall turn away <hi type="italic">their</hi> ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables. <hi type="super">5</hi> But watch thou in all things, endure afflictions, do the work of an evangelist, make full proof of thy ministry. <hi type="super">6</hi> For I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand. <hi type="super">7</hi> I have fought a good fight, I have finished <hi type="italic">my</hi> course, I have kept the faith: 8 Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing. <div eID="gen32554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32555" type="x-p"/> Observe, I. How awfully this charge is introduced (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">I charge thee before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, who shall judge the quick and the dead at his appearing and his kingdom.</hi> Observe, The best of men have need to be awed into the discharge of their duty. The work of a minister is not an indifferent thing, but absolutely necessary. Woe be to him if he preach not the gospel, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.16">1 Cor. ix. 16</reference>. To induce him to faithfulness, he must consider, 1. That the eye of God and Jesus Christ was upon him: <hi type="italic">I charge thee before God and the Lord Jesus Christ;</hi> that is, "as thou tenderest the favour of God and Jesus Christ; as thou wilt approve thyself to God and Jesus Christ, by the obligations both of natural and revealed religion; as thou wilt make due returns to the God who made thee and the Lord Jesus Christ who redeemed thee." 2. He charges him as he will answer it at the great day, reminding him of the judgment to come, which is committed to the Lord Jesus. He shall judge the quick and the dead <hi type="italic">at his appearing and his kingdom,</hi> that is, when he appears in his kingdom. It concerns all, both ministers and people, seriously to consider the account that they must shortly give to Jesus Christ of all the trusts reposed in them. Christ shall <hi type="italic">judge the quick and the dead,</hi> that is, those that at the last day shall be found alive, and those who shall be raised to life out of the grave. Note, (1.) The Lord Jesus Christ shall judge the quick and the dead. <hi type="italic">God hath committed all judgment unto the Son,</hi> and hath appointed him the Judge of quick and dead, <reference osisRef="Acts.10.42">Acts x. 42</reference>. (2.) He will appear; he will come the second time, and it will be a glorious appearance, as the word <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">epiphaneia</hi></hi> signifies. (3.) Then his kingdom shall appear in its glory: <hi type="italic">At his appearing and kingdom;</hi> for he will then appear in his kingdom, sitting on a throne, to judge the world. <div eID="gen32555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32556" type="x-p"/> II. What is the matter of the charge, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.2-2Tim.4.5">v. 2-5</reference>. He is charged, <div eID="gen32556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32557" type="x-p"/> 1. To <hi type="italic">preach the word.</hi> This is ministers' business; a dispensation is committed to them. It is not their own notions and fancies that they are to preach, but the pure plain word of God; and they must not corrupt it, but as of sincerity, but as of God, in the sight of God, they speak in Christ, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.17">2 Cor. ii. 17</reference>. <div eID="gen32557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32558" type="x-p"/> 2. To urge what he preached, and to press it with all earnestness upon his hearers: "<hi type="italic">Be instant in season and out of season, reprove, rebuke, exhort;</hi> do this work with all fervency of spirit. Call upon those under thy charge to take heed of sin, to do their duty: call upon them to repent, and believe, and live a holy life, and this both in season and out of season. <hi type="italic">In season,</hi> when they are at leisure to hear thee, when some special opportunity offers itself of speaking to them with advantage. Nay, do it <hi type="italic">out of season,</hi> even when there is not that apparent probability of fastening something upon them, because thou dost not know but the Spirit of God may fasten upon them; for the wind bloweth where it listeth; and <hi type="italic">in the morning we must sow our seed, and in the evening not withhold our hand,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.6">Eccl. xi. 6</reference>. We must do it in season, that is, let slip no opportunity; and do it out of season, that is, not shift off the duty, under pretence that it is out of season. <div eID="gen32558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32559" type="x-p"/> 3. He must tell people of their faults: "<hi type="italic">Reprove them, rebuke them.</hi> Convince wicked people of the evil and danger of their wicked courses. Endeavour, by dealing plainly with them, to bring them to repentance. Rebuke them with gravity and authority, in Christ's name, that they may take thy displeasure against them as an indication of God's displeasure." <div eID="gen32559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32560" type="x-p"/> 4. He must direct, encourage, and quicken those who began well. "<hi type="italic">Exhort them</hi> (persuade them to hold on, and endure to the end) and this <hi type="italic">with all long-suffering and doctrine.</hi>" (1.) He must do it very patiently: <hi type="italic">With all long-suffering.</hi> "If thou do not see the effect of thy labours presently, yet do not therefore give up the cause; be not weary of speaking to them." While God shows to them all long-suffering, let ministers exhort with all long-suffering. (2.) He must do it rationally, not with passion, but <hi type="italic">with doctrine,</hi> that is, "In order to the reducing of them to good practices, instil into them good principles. Teach them the truth as it is in Jesus, reduce them to a firm belief of it, and this will be a means both to reclaim them from evil and to bring them to good." Observe, [1.] A minister's work has various parts: he is to <hi type="italic">preach the word,</hi> to <hi type="italic">reprove, rebuke,</hi> and <hi type="italic">exhort.</hi> [2.] He is to be very diligent and careful; he must be <hi type="italic">instant in season and out of season;</hi> he must spare no pains nor labour, but must be urgent with them to take care of their souls and their eternal concerns. <div eID="gen32560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32561" type="x-p"/> 5. He must <hi type="italic">watch in all things.</hi> "Seek an opportunity of doing them a kindness; let no fair occasion slip, through thy negligence. Watch to thy work; watch against the temptations of Satan, by which thou mayest be diverted from it; watch over the souls of those who are committed to thy charge." <div eID="gen32561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32562" type="x-p"/> 6. He must count upon afflictions, and endure them, make the best of them. <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Kakopatheson,</hi></hi> endure <hi type="italic">patiently.</hi> "Be not discouraged by the difficulties thou meetest with, but bear them with an evenness of spirit. Inure thyself to hardships." <div eID="gen32562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32563" type="x-p"/> 7. He must remember his office, and discharge its duties: <hi type="italic">Do the work of an evangelist.</hi> The office of the evangelist was, as the apostles' deputies, to water the churches that they planted. They were not settled pastors, but for some time resided in, and presided over, the churches that the apostles had planted, till they were settled under a standing ministry. This was Timothy's work. <div eID="gen32563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32564" type="x-p"/> 8. He must fulfil his ministry: <hi type="italic">Make full proof of it.</hi> It was a great trust that was reposed in him, and therefore he must answer it, and perform all the parts of his office with diligence and care. Observe, (1.) A minister must expect afflictions in the faithful discharge of his duty. (2.) He must endure them patiently, like a Christian hero. (3.) These must not discourage him in his work, for he must do his work, and fulfil his ministry. (4.) The best way to make full proof of our ministry is to fulfil it, to fill it up in all its parts with proper work. <div eID="gen32564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32565" type="x-p"/> III. The reasons to enforce the charge. <div eID="gen32565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32566" type="x-p"/> 1. Because errors and heresies were likely to creep into the church, by which the minds of many professing Christians would be corrupted (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.3-2Tim.4.4">v. 3, 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine.</hi> Therefore improve the present time, when they will endure it. Be busy now, for it is seedtime; when the fields are white unto the harvest, put in the sickle, for the present gale of opportunity will be soon over. <hi type="italic">They will not endure sound doctrine.</hi> There will be those who will <hi type="italic">heap to themselves corrupt teachers, and will turn away their ears from the truth;</hi> and therefore secure as many as thou canst, that, when these storms and tempests do arise, they may be well fixed, and their apostasy may be prevented." People must hear, and ministers must preach, for the time to come, and guard against the mischiefs that are likely to arise hereafter, though they do not yet arise. They will <hi type="italic">turn away their ears from the truth;</hi> they will grow weary of the old plain gospel of Christ, and then they will be greedy of fables, and take pleasure in them, and God will give them up to those strong delusions, because they received not the truth in the love of it, <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.11-2Thess.2.12">2 Thess. ii. 11, 12</reference>. Observe, (1.) These teachers were of their own heaping up, and not of God's sending; but they chose them, to gratify their lusts, and to please their itching ears. (2.) People do so when they will not endure sound doctrine, that preaching which is searching, plain, and to the purpose; then they will have teachers of their own. (3.) There is a wide difference between the word of God and the word of such teachers; the one is sound doctrine, the word of truth, the other is only fables. (4.) Those that are turned unto fables first turn away their ears from the truth, for they cannot hear and mind both, any more than they can serve two masters. Nay, further, it is said, <hi type="italic">They shall be turned unto fables.</hi> God justly suffers those to turn to fables who grow weary of the truth, and gives them up to be led aside from the truth by fables. <div eID="gen32566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32567" type="x-p"/> 2. Because Paul for his part had almost done his work: <hi type="italic">Do thou make full proof of thy ministry, for I am now ready to be offered,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.6">v. 6</reference>. And, <div eID="gen32567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32568" type="x-p"/> (1.) "Therefore there will be the more occasion for thee." When labourers are removed out of the vineyard, it is no time for those to loiter that are left behind, but to double their diligence. The fewer hands there are to work the more industrious those hands must be that are at work. <div eID="gen32568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32569" type="x-p"/> (2.) "I have done the work of my day and generation; do thou in like manner do the work of thy day and generation." <div eID="gen32569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32570" type="x-p"/> (3.) The comfort and cheerfulness of Paul, in the prospect of his approaching departure, might encourage Timothy to the utmost industry, and diligence, and seriousness in his work. Paul was an old soldier of Jesus Christ, Timothy was but newly enlisted. "Come," says Paul, "I have found our Master kind and the cause good; I can look back upon my warfare with a great deal of pleasure and satisfaction; and therefore be not afraid of the difficulties thou must meet with. The crown of life is as sure to thee as if it were already upon thy head; and therefore endure afflictions, and make full proof of thy ministry." The courage and comfort of dying saints and ministers, and especially dying martyrs, are a great confirmation of the truth of the Christian religion, and a great encouragement to living saints and ministers in their work. Here the apostle looks forward, upon his death approaching: <hi type="italic">I am now ready to be offered.</hi> The Holy Ghost witnessed in every city that bonds and afflictions did abide him, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.23">Acts xx. 23</reference>. He was now at Rome, and it is probable that he had particular intimations from the Spirit that there he should seal the truth with his blood; and he looks upon it now as near at hand: I am <hi type="italic">already poured out;</hi> so it is in the original, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ede spendomai;</hi></hi> that is, I am already a martyr in affection. It alludes to the pouring out of the drink-offerings; for the blood of the martyrs, though it was not a sacrifice of atonement, was a sacrifice of acknowledgment to the honour of the grace of God and his truths. Observe, <div eID="gen32570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32571" type="x-p"/> [1.] With what pleasure he speaks of dying. He calls it his departure; though it is probable that he foresaw he must die a violent bloody death, yet he calls it his departure, or his release. Death to a good man is his release from the imprisonment of this world and his departure to the enjoyments of another world; he does not cease to be, but is only removed from one world to another. <div eID="gen32571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32572" type="x-p"/> [2.] With what pleasure he looks back upon the life he had lived (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course,</hi> &c. He did not fear death, because he had the testimony of his conscience that by the grace of God he had in some measure answered the ends of living. As a Christian, as a minister, he had fought a good fight. He had done the service, gone through the difficulties of his warfare, and had been instrumental in carrying on the glorious victories of the exalted Redeemer over the powers of darkness. His life was a course, and he had now finished it; as his warfare was accomplished, so his race was run. "<hi type="italic">I have kept the faith.</hi> I have kept the doctrines of the gospel, and never betrayed any of them." Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The life of a Christian, but especially of a minister, is a warfare and a race, sometimes compared to the one in the scripture, and sometimes to the other. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is a good fight, a good warfare; the cause is good, and the victory is sure, if we continue faithful and courageous. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> We must fight this good fight; we must fight it out, and finish our course; we must not give over till we are made more than conquerors through him who hath loved us, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.37">Rom. viii. 37</reference>. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> It is a great comfort to a dying saint, when he can look back upon his past life and say with our apostle, "<hi type="italic">I have fought,</hi> &c. I have kept the faith, the doctrine of faith and the grace of faith." Towards the end of our days to be able to speak in this manner, what comfort, unspeakable comfort, will it afford! Let it then be our constant endeavour, by the grace of God, that we may finish our course with joy, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.24">Acts xx. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen32572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32573" type="x-p"/> [3.] With what pleasure he looks forward to the life he was to live hereafter (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness,</hi> &c. He had lost for Christ, but he was sure he should not lose by him, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.8">Phil. iii. 8</reference>. Let this encourage Timothy to endure hardness as a good soldier of Jesus Christ that there is a crown of life before us, the glory and joy of which will abundantly recompense all the hardships and toils of our present warfare. Observe, It is called <hi type="italic">a crown of righteousness,</hi> because it will be the recompence of our services, which <hi type="italic">God is not unrighteous to forget;</hi> and because our holiness and righteousness will there be perfected, and will be our crown. God will give it as <hi type="italic">a righteous Judge,</hi> who will let none love by him. And yet this crown of righteousness was not peculiar to Paul, as if it belonged only to apostles and eminent ministers and martyrs, but <hi type="italic">to all those also that love his appearing.</hi> Observe, It is the character of all the saints that they love the appearing of Jesus Christ: they loved his first appearing, when he appeared to take away sin by the sacrifice of himself (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.26">Heb. ix. 26</reference>); they love to think of it; they love his second appearing at the great day; love it, and long for it: and, with respect to those who love the appearing of Jesus Christ, he shall appear to their joy; there is a crown of righteousness reserved for them, which shall then be given them, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.28">Heb. ix. 28</reference>. We learn hence, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The Lord is the righteous Judge, for his judgment is according to truth. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The crown of believers is a crown of righteousness, purchased by the righteousness of Christ, and bestowed as the reward of the saints' righteousness. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> This crown, which believers shall wear, is laid up for them; they have it not at present, for here they are but heirs; they have it not in possession, and yet it is sure, for it is laid up for them. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> The righteous Judge will give it to all who love, prepare, and long for his appearing. <hi type="italic">Surely I come quickly. Amen, even so come, Lord Jesus.</hi>
entries.27fb35a053870962d3078a078517cf1769d254cf: <div eID="gen32573" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle's Directions to Timothy. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen32574" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> Do thy diligence to come shortly unto me: 10 For Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world, and is departed unto Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia, Titus unto Dalmatia. <hi type="super">11</hi> Only Luke is with me. Take Mark, and bring him with thee: for he is profitable to me for the ministry. 12 And Tychicus have I sent to Ephesus. <hi type="super">13</hi> The cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring <hi type="italic">with thee,</hi> and the books, <hi type="italic">but</hi> especially the parchments. 14 Alexander the coppersmith did me much evil: the Lord reward him according to his works: <hi type="super">15</hi> Of whom be thou ware also; for he hath greatly withstood our words. <div eID="gen32574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32575" type="x-p"/> Here are divers particular matters which Paul mentions to Timothy, now at the closing of the epistle. 1. He bids him hasten to him, if possible (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">So thy diligence to come shortly to me.</hi> For Timothy was an evangelist, one who was not a fixed pastor of any one place, but attended the motions of the apostles, to build upon their foundation. Paul wanted Timothy's company and help; and the reason he gives is because several had left him (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.10">v. 10</reference>); one from an ill principle, namely, <hi type="italic">Demas,</hi> who abides under an ill name for it: <hi type="italic">Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world.</hi> He quitted Paul and his interest, either for fear of suffering (because Paul was now a prisoner, and he was afraid of coming into trouble upon his account) or being called off from his ministry by secular affairs, in which he entangled himself; his first love to Christ and his gospel was forsaken and forgotten, and he fell in love with the world. Note, Love to this present world is often the cause of apostasy from the truths and ways of Jesus Christ. He has gone off, has <hi type="italic">departed to Thessalonica,</hi> called thither perhaps by trade, or by some other worldly business. <hi type="italic">Crescens</hi> had gone one way and <hi type="italic">Titus</hi> another way. <hi type="italic">Luke</hi> however remained with Paul (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.11-2Tim.4.12">v. 11, 12</reference>), and was not this enough? Paul did not think it so; he loved the company of his friends. 2. He speaks respectfully concerning <hi type="italic">Mark: He is profitable to me for the ministry.</hi> It is supposed that this Mark was he about whom Paul and Barnabas had contended, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.39">Acts xv. 39</reference>. Paul would not take him with him to the work, because he had once flinched and drawn back: but now, says he, <hi type="italic">Take Mark, and bring him with thee.</hi> By this it appears that Paul was now reconciled to Mark, and had a better opinion of him than he had had formerly. This teaches us to be of a forgiving spirit; we must not therefore disclaim for ever making use of those that are profitable and useful, though they may have done amiss. 3. Paul orders Timothy to come to him, bids him as he came through Troas to bring with him thence those things which he had left behind him there (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.13">v. 13</reference>), the cloak he had left there, which, it may be, Paul had the more occasion for in a cold prison. It is probable that it was the habit Paul usually wore, a plain dress. Some read it, the <hi type="italic">roll of parchment I left at Troas;</hi> others, the <hi type="italic">desk</hi> that I left. Paul was guided by divine inspiration, and yet he would have his books with him. Whereas he had exhorted Timothy to give attendance to reading, so he did himself, though he was now ready to be offered. As long as we live, we must be still learning. <hi type="italic">But especially the parchments,</hi> which some think were the originals of his epistles; others think they were the skins of which he made his tents, whereby he obtained a livelihood, working with his own hands. 4. He mentions <hi type="italic">Alexander,</hi> and the mischief that he had done him, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.14-2Tim.4.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. This is he who is spoken of <reference osisRef="Acts.19.33">Acts xix. 33</reference>. It should seem, he had been a professor of the Christian religion, a forward professor, for he was there particularly maligned by the worshippers of Diana, and yet he did Paul much evil. Paul was in as much danger from false brethren (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.26">2 Cor. xi. 26</reference>) as from open enemies. Paul foretels that God would reckon with him. It is a prophetical denunciation of the just judgment of God that would befal him: The Lord <hi type="italic">will reward him according to his works.</hi> He cautions Timothy to take heed of him: "<hi type="italic">Of whom be thou aware also,</hi> that he do not, under pretence of friendship, betray thee to mischief." It is dangerous having any thing to do with those who would be enemies to such a man as Paul. Observe, (1.) Some who were once Paul's hearers and admirers did not give him reason to remember them with much pleasure; for one forsook him, and another did him much evil, and greatly withstood his words. Yet, (2.) At the same time he mentions some with pleasure; the badness of some did not make him forget the goodness of others; such as <hi type="italic">Timothy, Titus, Mark,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Luke.</hi> (3.) The apostle has left a brand on the names and memory of two persons; the one is <hi type="italic">Demas,</hi> who forsook him, having loved the present world, and the other is <hi type="italic">Alexander,</hi> who greatly withstood his words. (4.) God will reward evil-doers, particularly apostates, according to their works. (5.) Of such as are of Alexander's spirit and temper we should beware; for they will do us no good, but all the mischief that is in their power.
entries.5acf5af2f26a3c2b9c1431542d77e930a0ae5d2e: <div eID="gen32575" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle's Directions to Timothy; Salutations and Benedictions. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen32576" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> At my first answer no man stood with me, but all <hi type="italic">men</hi> forsook me: <hi type="italic">I pray God</hi> that it may not be laid to their charge. <hi type="super">17</hi> Notwithstanding the Lord stood with me, and strengthened me; that by me the preaching might be fully known, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> all the Gentiles might hear: and I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion. <hi type="super">18</hi> And the Lord shall deliver me from every evil work, and will preserve <hi type="italic">me</hi> unto his heavenly kingdom: to whom <hi type="italic">be</hi> glory for ever and ever. Amen. <hi type="super">19</hi> Salute Prisca and Aquila, and the household of Onesiphorus. <hi type="super">20</hi> Erastus abode at Corinth: but Trophimus have I left at Miletum sick. <hi type="super">21</hi> Do thy diligence to come before winter. Eubulus greeteth thee, and Pudens, and Linus, and Claudia, and all the brethren. <hi type="super">22</hi> The Lord Jesus Christ <hi type="italic">be</hi> with thy spirit. Grace <hi type="italic">be</hi> with you. Amen. <div eID="gen32576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32577" type="x-p"/> Here, I. He gives Timothy an account of his own present circumstances. <div eID="gen32577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32578" type="x-p"/> 1. He had lately been called to appear before the emperor, upon his appeal to Cæsar; and then <hi type="italic">no man stood with him</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.16">v. 16</reference>), to plead his cause, to bear testimony for him, or so much as to keep him in countenance, but <hi type="italic">all men forsook him.</hi> This was strange, that so good a man as Paul should have nobody to own him, even at Rome, where there were many Christians, whose faith was spoken of throughout the world, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.8">Rom. i. 8</reference>. But men are but men. The Christians at Rome were forward to go and meet him (<reference osisRef="Acts.28.1-Acts.28.31">Acts xxviii.</reference>); but when it came to the pinch, and they would be in danger of suffering with him, then they all forsook him. He prays that God would not lay it to their charge, intimating that it was a great fault, and God might justly be angry with them, but he prays God to forgive them. See what a distinction is put between sins of presumption and sins of infirmity. Alexander the coppersmith, who maliciously withstood Paul, he prays against: <hi type="italic">The Lord reward him according to his works;</hi> but respecting these Christians, who through weakness shrunk from Paul in time of trial, he says, <hi type="italic">The Lord lay it not to their charge.</hi> Observe, (1.) Paul had his trials in his friends' forsaking him in a time of danger as well as in the opposition made by enemies: all forsook him. (2.) It was their sin not to appear for the good apostle, especially at his first answer; but it was a sin of weakness, and therefore the more excusable. Yet, (3.) God might lay it to their charge, but Paul endeavours to prevent it by his earnest prayers: <hi type="italic">Let it not be laid to their charge.</hi> <div eID="gen32578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32579" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">Notwithstanding this God stood by him</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.17">v. 17</reference>), gave him extraordinary wisdom and courage, to enable him to speak so much the better himself. When he had nobody to keep him in countenance, God made his face to shine.—<hi type="italic">That by me the preaching might be fully known,</hi> that is, "God brought me out from that difficulty that I might preach the gospel, which is my business." Nay, it should seem, that he might preach the gospel at that time; for Paul knew how to preach at the bar as well as in the pulpit. <hi type="italic">And that all the Gentiles might hear;</hi> the emperor himself and the great men who would never have heard Paul preach if he had not been brought before them. <hi type="italic">And I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion,</hi> that is, of Nero (as some think) or some other judge. Some understand it only as a proverbial form of speech, to signify that he was in imminent danger. <hi type="italic">And the Lord shall deliver me from every evil work.</hi> See how Paul improved his experiences: "<hi type="italic">He that delivered doth deliver, and we trust he will yet deliver,</hi> will deliver me <hi type="italic">from every evil work,</hi> from any ill done to me by others. <hi type="italic">And shall preserve me to his heavenly kingdom.</hi>" And for this he gives glory to God, rejoicing in hope of the glory of God. Observe, (1.) If the Lord stand by us, he will strengthen us, in a time of difficulty and danger, and his presence will more than supply every one's absence. (2.) When the Lord preserves his servants from great and imminent danger, it is for eminent work and service. Paul was preserved that by him the preaching might be fully known, &c. (3.) Former deliverances should encourage future hopes. (4.) There is a heavenly kingdom, to which the Lord will preserve his faithful witnessing or suffering servants. (5.) We ought to give God the glory of all past, present, and future deliverances: <hi type="italic">To whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.</hi> <div eID="gen32579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32580" type="x-p"/> II. He sends salutations to <hi type="italic">Aquila, and Priscilla, and the household of Onesiphorus,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.19">v. 19</reference>. He mentions his leaving <hi type="italic">Trophimus sick at Miletum</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.20">v. 20</reference>), by which it appears that though the apostles healed all manner of diseases miraculously, for the confirmation of their doctrine, yet they did not exert that power upon their own friends, lest it should have looked like a collusion. <div eID="gen32580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32581" type="x-p"/> III. He hastens Timothy to <hi type="italic">come to him before winter</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.21">v. 21</reference>), because he longed to see him, and because in the winter the journey or voyage would be more dangerous. <div eID="gen32581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32582" type="x-p"/> IV. He sends commendations to him from <hi type="italic">Eubulus, Pudens, Linus, Claudia,</hi> and all the <hi type="italic">brethren.</hi> One of the heathen writers at this time mentions one Pudens and his wife Claudia, and says the Claudia was a Briton, whence some have gathered that it was this Pudens, and that Claudia here was his wife, and that they were eminent Christians at Rome. <div eID="gen32582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32583" type="x-p"/> V. He concludes with a prayer, that the <hi type="italic">Lord Jesus would be with his spirit.</hi> We need no more to make us happy than to have the Lord Jesus Christ with our spirits; for in him all spiritual blessings are summed up. And it is the best prayer we can put up for our friends, that the Lord Jesus Christ may be with their spirits, to sanctify and save them, and at last to receive them to himself; as Stephen the proto-martyr prayed, <hi type="italic">Lord Jesus, receive my spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.7.59">Acts vii. 59</reference>. "Lord Jesus, receive that spirit which thou hast been with while it was united to the body; do not now leave it in its separate state." <hi type="italic">Grace be with you. Amen.</hi> This was our apostle's token in every epistle; so he wrote. <hi type="italic">The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.17-2Thess.3.18">2 Thess. iii. 17, 18</reference>. And if grace be with us here to convert and change us, to make us holy, to keep us humble, and to enable us to persevere to the end, glory will crown us hereafter: <hi type="italic">for the Lord is a sun, and a shield; the Lord will give grace and glory, and no good thing will he withhold from those that walk uprightly. O Lord of hosts, blessed is the man that trusteth in thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.84.11-Ps.84.12">Ps. lxxxiv. 11, 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">Now unto the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God our Saviour, be honour and glory for ever and ever.</hi> Amen.  <chapter eID="2Tim.4"/> <div eID="gen32583" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen32479" osisID="2Tim" type="book"/>

entries.a1f3f07ef8b67146ef0c5f7b0776d8b72cddff7b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18229"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <div sID="gen37785" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.1-2Tim.4.22">2Ti 4:1-22</reference>. Solemn Charge to Timothy to Do His Duty Zealously, for Times of Apostasy Are at Hand, and the Apostle Is near His Triumphant End: Requests Him to Come and Bring Mark with Him to Rome, as Luke Alone Is with Him, the Others Having Gone: Also His Cloak and Parchments: Warns Him against Alexander: Tells What Befell Him at His First Defense: Greetings: Benediction.<div eID="gen37785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37786" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18229"/><hi type="bold">1. charge--</hi>Greek, "adjure."<div eID="gen37786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37787" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">therefore--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts.<div eID="gen37787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37788" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord Jesus Christ--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read simply, "Christ Jesus."<div eID="gen37788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37789" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall judge--</hi>His commission from God is mentioned, <reference osisRef="Acts.10.42">Ac 10:42</reference>; his resolution to do so, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.5">1Pe 4:5</reference>; the execution of his commission, here.<div eID="gen37789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37790" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at his appearing--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "and" for "at"; then translate, "(I charge thee before God ... ) and by His appearing."<div eID="gen37790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37791" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and his kingdom--</hi>to be set at His appearing, when we hope to reign with Him. His kingdom is real now, but not visible. It shall then be both real and visible (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.18">Lu 22:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.22.30">30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.7">Re 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.15">11:15</reference>; 19:6). Now he reigns in the midst of His enemies expecting till they shall be overthrown (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.2">Psa 110:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.13">He 10:13</reference>). Then He shall reign with His adversaries prostrate. <div eID="gen37791" type="x-p"/>
entries.839a80babdf94a477022a2fa99a9d233dd0aa9d7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18230"/><div sID="gen37792" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18230"/><hi type="bold">2. Preach--</hi>literally, "proclaim as a herald." The term for the discourses in the synagogue was daraschoth; the corresponding Greek term (implying dialectial style, dialogue, and discussion, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.2">Ac 17:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.18.4">18:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.18.19">19</reference>) is applied in Acts to discourses in the Christian Church. Justin Martyr [Apology, 2], describes the order of public worship, "On Sunday all meet and the writings of the apostles and prophets are read; then the president delivers a discourse; after this all stand up and pray; then there is offered bread and wine and water; the president likewise prays and gives thanks, and the people solemnly assent, saying, Amen." The bishops and presbyters had the right and duty to preach, but they sometimes called on deacons, and even laymen, to preach. Eusebius [Ecclesiastical History, 6.19]; in this the Church imitated the synagogue (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.17-Luke.4.22">Lu 4:17-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.15">Ac 13:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.16">16</reference>).<div eID="gen37792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37793" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be instant--</hi>that is, urgent, earnest, in the whole work of the ministry.<div eID="gen37793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37794" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in season, out of season--</hi>that is, at all seasons; whether they regard your speaking as seasonable or unseasonable. "Just as the fountains, though none may draw from them, still flow on; and the rivers, though none drink of them, still run; so must we do all on our part in speaking, though none give heed to us" [Chrysostom, Homily, 30, vol. 5., p. 221]. I think with Chrysostom, there is included also the idea of times whether seasonable or unseasonable to Timothy himself; not merely when convenient, but when inconvenient to thee, night as well as day (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.31">Ac 20:31</reference>), in danger as well as in safety, in prison and when doomed to death as well as when at large, not only in church, but everywhere and on all occasions, whenever and wherever the Lord's work requires it.<div eID="gen37794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37795" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reprove--</hi>"convict," "confute."<div eID="gen37795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37796" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with, &c.--</hi>Greek, "IN (the element in which the exhortation ought to have place) all long-suffering (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.24">2Ti 2:24</reference>, 25; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.10">3:10</reference>) and teaching"; compare <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.24">2Ti 2:24</reference>, "apt to teach." The Greek for "doctrine" here is didache, but in <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.16">2Ti 3:16</reference>, didascalia. "Didascalia" is what one receives; "didache" is what is communicated [Tittmann]. <div eID="gen37796" type="x-p"/>
entries.b4fde77480193e24c530f8fe4eecc7c6313a3c61: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18231"/><div sID="gen37797" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18231"/><hi type="bold">3. they--</hi>professing Christians.<div eID="gen37797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37798" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sound doctrine--</hi>Greek, "the sound (see on <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.10">1Ti 1:10</reference>) doctrine (didascalias)" or "teaching," namely, of the Gospel. Presently follows the concrete, "teachers."<div eID="gen37798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37799" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">after their own lusts--</hi>Instead of regarding the will of God they dislike being interrupted in their lusts by true teachers.<div eID="gen37799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37800" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heap--</hi>one on another: an indiscriminate mass of false teachers. Variety delights itching ears. "He who despises sound teaching, leaves sound teachers; they seek instructors like themselves" [Bengel]. It is the corruption of the people in the first instance, that creates priestcraft (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.1">Ex 32:1</reference>).<div eID="gen37800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37801" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to themselves--</hi>such as will suit their depraved tastes; populus vult decipi, et decipiatur--"the people wish to be deceived, so let them be deceived." "Like priest, like people" (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.31">1Ki 12:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.4.9">Ho 4:9</reference>).<div eID="gen37801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37802" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">itching--</hi>like to hear teachers who give them mere pleasure (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.19-Acts.17.21">Ac 17:19-21</reference>), and do not offend by truths grating to their ears. They, as it were, tickle with pleasure the levity of the multitude [Cicero], who come as to a theater to hear what will delight their ears, not to learn [Seneca, Epistles, 10.8] what will do them good. "Itch in the ear is as bad in any other part of the body, and perhaps worse" [South]. <div eID="gen37802" type="x-p"/>
entries.871cab8ad851d4316909c57e48dc4bc6005b958e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18232"/><div sID="gen37803" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18232"/>4. The ear brooks not what is opposed to the man's lusts.<div eID="gen37803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37804" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">turned--</hi>Greek, "turned aside" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.6">1Ti 1:6</reference>). It is a righteous retribution, that when men turn away from the truth, they should be turned to fables (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.19">Jr 2:19</reference>).<div eID="gen37804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37805" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fables--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.4">1Ti 1:4</reference>). <div eID="gen37805" type="x-p"/>
entries.b42f0a8c44e2ce3b8b8805da04cdd9eb9e75cc27: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18233"/><div sID="gen37806" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18233"/>5. I am no longer here to withstand these things; be thou a worthy successor of me, no longer depending on me for counsel, but thine own master, and swimming without the corks [Calvin]; follow my steps, inherit their result, and the honor of their end [Alford].<div eID="gen37806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37807" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">watch thou--</hi>literally, "with the wakefulness of one sober."<div eID="gen37807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37808" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in all things--</hi>on all occasions and under all circumstances (<reference osisRef="Titus.2.7">Tit 2:7</reference>).<div eID="gen37808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37809" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">endure affliction--</hi>suffer hardships [Alford].<div eID="gen37809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37810" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">evangelist--</hi>a missionary bishop preacher, and teacher.<div eID="gen37810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37811" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make full proof of--</hi>fulfil in all its requirements, leaving nothing undone (<reference osisRef="Acts.12.25">Ac 12:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.15.19">Ro 15:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.4.17">Col 4:17</reference>). <div eID="gen37811" type="x-p"/>
entries.110452401d65f34147364313dbac27ed94345647: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18234"/><div sID="gen37812" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18234"/><hi type="bold">6. Greek, "For I am already being offered"; literally, as a libation; appropriate to the shedding of his blood. Every sacrifice began with an initiatory libation on the victim's head (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Phil.2.17">Php 2:17</reference>). A motive to stimulate Timothy to faithfulness--</hi>the departure and final blessedness of Paul; it is the end that crowns the work [Bengel]. As the time of his departure was indicated to Peter, so to Paul (<reference osisRef="2Pet.1.14">2Pe 1:14</reference>).<div eID="gen37812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37813" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my departure--</hi>literally, "loosing anchor" (see on <reference osisRef="Phil.1.23">Php 1:23</reference>). Dissolution. <div eID="gen37813" type="x-p"/>
entries.0096610dc7e8713245284a47071e0249867938ae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18235"/><div sID="gen37814" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18235"/>7. "I have striven the good strife"; the Greek is not restricted to a fight, but includes any competitive contest, for example, that of the racecourse (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.12">1Ti 6:12</reference> [Alford]; <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.24">1Co 9:24</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.1">He 12:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.2">2</reference>).<div eID="gen37814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37815" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">kept the faith--</hi>the Christian faith committed to me as a believer and an apostle (compare <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.14">2Ti 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.2.10">Re 2:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.10">3:10</reference>). <div eID="gen37815" type="x-p"/>
entries.631e1f8cfe9a8f05fd89c1432202e91095dbdfef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18236"/><div sID="gen37816" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18236"/><hi type="bold">8. a crown--</hi>rather as Greek, "the crown." The "henceforth" marks the decisive moment; he looks to his state in a threefold aspect: (1) The past "I have fought"; (2) The immediate present; "there is laid up for me." (3) The future "the Lord will give in that day" [Bengel].<div eID="gen37816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37817" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">crown--</hi>a crown, or garland, used to be bestowed at the Greek national games on the successful competitor in wrestling, running, &c. (compare <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.4">1Pe 5:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.2.10">Re 2:10</reference>).<div eID="gen37817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37818" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of righteousness--</hi>The reward is in recognition of righteousness wrought in Paul by God's Spirit; the crown is prepared for the righteous; but it is a crown which consists in righteousness. Righteousness will be its own reward (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.11">Re 22:11</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Exod.39.30">Ex 39:30</reference>. A man is justified gratuitously by the merits of Christ through faith; and when he is so justified God accepts his works and honors them with a reward which is not their due, but is given of grace. "So great is God's goodness to men that He wills that their works should be merits, though they are merely His own gifts" [Pope Celestine I., Epistles, 12].<div eID="gen37818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37819" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">give--</hi>Greek, "shall award" in righteous requital as "Judge" (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.31">Ac 17:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.10">2Co 5:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.6">2Th 1:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.7">7</reference>).<div eID="gen37819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37820" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in that day--</hi>not until His appearing (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.12">2Ti 1:12</reference>). The partakers of the first resurrection may receive a crown also at the last day, and obtain in that general assembly of all men, a new award of praise. The favorable sentence passed on the "brethren" of the Judge, who sit with Him on His throne, is in <reference osisRef="Matt.25.40">Mt 25:40</reference>, taken for granted as already awarded, when that affecting those who benefited them is being passed [Bengel]. The former, the elect Church who reign with Christ in the millennium, are fewer than the latter. The righteous heavenly Judge stands in contrast to the unrighteous earthly judges who condemned Paul.<div eID="gen37820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37821" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">me--</hi>individual appropriation. Greek, "not only to me."<div eID="gen37821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37822" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them that love--</hi>Greek, "have loved, and do love"; habitual love and desire for Christ's appearing, which presupposes faith (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.9.28">He 9:28</reference>). Compare the sad contrast, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.10">2Ti 4:10</reference>, "having loved this present world." <div eID="gen37822" type="x-p"/>
entries.e234c46c338a6799c6f1a7fe15f50960bbb246f7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18237"/><div sID="gen37823" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18237"/>9. (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.21">2Ti 4:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.4">2Ti 1:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.8">8</reference>.) Timothy is asked to come to be a comfort to Paul, and also to be strengthened by Paul, for carrying on the Gospel work after Paul's decease. <div eID="gen37823" type="x-p"/>
entries.d387ffcbcafb16b632721dcef4510afd68c1e0c1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18238"/><div sID="gen37824" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18238"/><hi type="bold">10. Demas--</hi>once a "fellow laborer" of Paul, along with Mark and Luke (<reference osisRef="Col.4.14">Col 4:14</reference>; Phm 24). His motive for forsaking Paul seems to have been love of worldly ease, safety, and comforts at home, and disinclination to brave danger with Paul (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.20">Mt 13:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.22">21, 22</reference>). Chrysostom implies that Thessalonica was his home.<div eID="gen37824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37825" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Galatia--</hi>One oldest manuscript supports the reading "Gaul." But most oldest manuscripts, &c., "Galatia."<div eID="gen37825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37826" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Titus--</hi>He must have therefore left Crete after "setting in order" the affairs of the churches there (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.5">Tit 1:5</reference>).<div eID="gen37826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37827" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Dalmatia--</hi>part of the Roman province of Illyricum on the coast of the Adriatic. Paul had written to him (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.12">Tit 3:12</reference>) to come to him in the winter to Nicopolis (in Epirus), intending in the spring to preach the Gospel in the adjoining province of Dalmatia. Titus seems to have gone thither to carry out the apostle's intention, the execution of which was interrupted by his arrest. Whether he went of his own accord, as is likely, or was sent by Paul, which the expression "is departed" hardly accords with, cannot be positively decided. Paul here speaks only of his personal attendants having forsaken him; he had still friends among the Roman Christians who visited him (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.21">2Ti 4:21</reference>), though they had been afraid to stand by him at his trial (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.16">2Ti 4:16</reference>). <div eID="gen37827" type="x-p"/>
entries.c2802205ae23a0e4dafb338aa710294f9e642b2b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18239"/><div sID="gen37828" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18239"/><hi type="bold">11. Take--</hi>Greek, "take up" on thy journey (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.13">Ac 20:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.14">14</reference>). John Mark was probably in, or near, Colosse, as in the Epistle to the Colossians (<reference osisRef="Col.4.10">Col 4:10</reference>), written two years before this, he is mentioned as about to visit them. Timothy was now absent from Ephesus and somewhere in the interior of Asia Minor; hence he would be sure to fall in with Mark on his journey.<div eID="gen37828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37829" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he is profitable to me for the ministry--</hi>Mark had been under a cloud for having forsaken Paul at a critical moment in his missionary tour with Barnabas (Ac 15:37-40; 13:<reference osisRef="Acts.5.13">5, 13</reference>). Timothy had subsequently occupied the same post in relation to Paul as Mark once held. Hence Paul, appropriately here, wipes out the past censure by high praise of Mark and guards against Timothy's making self-complacent comparisons between himself and Mark, as though he were superior to the latter (compare Phm 24). Demas apostatizes. Mark returns to the right way, and is no longer unprofitable, but is profitable for the Gospel ministry (Phm 11). <div eID="gen37829" type="x-p"/>
entries.350562b41cc7898fb25dd71c18b0319491082bc4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18240"/><div sID="gen37830" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18240"/><hi type="bold">12. And--</hi>Greek, "But." Thou art to come to me, but Tychicus I have sent to Ephesus to supply thy place (if thou so willest it) in presiding over the Church there in thy absence (compare <reference osisRef="Titus.3.12">Tit 3:12</reference>). It is possible Tychicus was the bearer of this Epistle, though the omission of "to thee" is rather against this view. <div eID="gen37830" type="x-p"/>
entries.8aca41e9fd9435e271c767513c7d63a386efa837: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18241"/><div sID="gen37831" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18241"/><hi type="bold">13. cloak ... I left--</hi>probably obliged to leave it in a hurried departure from Troas.<div eID="gen37831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37832" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Carpus--</hi>a faithful friend to have been entrusted with so precious deposits. The mention of his "cloak," so far from being unworthy of inspiration, is one of those graphic touches which sheds a flood of light on the last scene of Paul's life, on the confines of two worlds; in this wanting a cloak to cover him from the winter cold, in that covered with the righteousness of saints, "clothed upon with his house from heaven" [Gaussen]. So the inner vesture and outer garment of Jesus, Paul's master, are suggestive of most instructive thought (<reference osisRef="John.19.2">Joh 19:2</reference>).<div eID="gen37832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37833" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">books--</hi>He was anxious respecting these that he might transmit them to the faithful, so that they might have the teaching of his writings when he should be gone.<div eID="gen37833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37834" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">especially the parchments--</hi>containing perhaps some of his inspired Epistles themselves. <div eID="gen37834" type="x-p"/>
entries.ecf9b04b7230b859e17a916a24901086a6d7d491: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18242"/><div sID="gen37835" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18242"/><hi type="bold">14. Alexander the coppersmith--</hi>or "smith" in general. Perhaps the same as the Alexander (see on <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.20">1Ti 1:20</reference>) at Ephesus. Excommunicated then he subsequently was restored, and now vented his personal malice because of his excommunication in accusing Paul before the Roman judges, whether of incendiarism or of introducing a new religion. See my Introduction. He may have been the Alexander put forward by the Jews in the tumult at Ephesus (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.33">Ac 19:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.19.34">34</reference>).<div eID="gen37835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37836" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reward--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "shall reward," or "requite him." Personal revenge certainly did not influence the apostle (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.16">2Ti 4:16</reference>, end). <div eID="gen37836" type="x-p"/>
entries.7c692b7edcccd7a5e5c2ae5525980d09e404fa26: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18243"/><div sID="gen37837" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18243"/><hi type="bold">15. our words--</hi>the arguments of us Christians for our common faith. Believers have a common cause. <div eID="gen37837" type="x-p"/>
entries.48e036f8e2b02b3d44cdc737a744f3325591147e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18244"/><div sID="gen37838" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18244"/><hi type="bold">16. At my first answer--</hi>that is, "defense" in court, at my first public examination. Timothy knew nothing of this, it is plain, till Paul now informs him. But during his former imprisonment at Rome, Timothy was with him (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.1">Php 1:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.7">7</reference>). This must have been, therefore, a second imprisonment. He must have been set free before the persecution in A.D. 64, when the Christians were accused of causing the conflagration in Rome; for, had he been a prisoner then, he certainly would not have been spared. The tradition [Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, 2.251] that he was finally beheaded, accords with his not having been put to death in the persecution, A.D. 64, when burning to death was the mode by which the Christians were executed, but subsequently to it. His "first" trial in his second imprisonment seems to have been on the charge of complicity in the conflagration; his absence from Rome may have been the ground of his acquittal on that charge; his final condemnation was probably on the charge of introducing a new and unlawful religion into Rome.<div eID="gen37838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37839" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stood with me--</hi>Greek, "came forward with me" [Alford] as a friend and advocate.<div eID="gen37839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37840" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">may it not be laid to their charge--</hi>The position of "their," in the Greek, is emphatic. "May it not be laid to THEIR charge," for they were intimidated; their drawing back from me was not from bad disposition so much as from fear; it is sure to be laid to the charge of those who intimidated them. Still Paul, like Stephen, would doubtless have offered the same prayer for his persecutors themselves (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.60">Ac 7:60</reference>). <div eID="gen37840" type="x-p"/>
entries.1ee8718d4e3af7773a86e8c979073e81e4b0b46b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18245"/><div sID="gen37841" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18245"/><hi type="bold">17. the Lord--</hi>the more because men deserted me.<div eID="gen37841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37842" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stood with me--</hi>stronger than "came forward with me" (Greek, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.16">2Ti 4:16</reference>).<div eID="gen37842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37843" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strengthened--</hi>Greek, "put strength in me."<div eID="gen37843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37844" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by me--</hi>"through me"; through my means. One single occasion is often of the greatest moment.<div eID="gen37844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37845" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the preaching--</hi>"the Gospel proclamation."<div eID="gen37845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37846" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">might be fully known--</hi>might be fully made (see on <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.5">2Ti 4:5</reference>).<div eID="gen37846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37847" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that all the Gentiles--</hi>present at my trial, "might hear" the Gospel proclaimed then. Rome was the capital of the Gentile world, so that a proclamation of the truth to the Romans was likely to go forth to the rest of the Gentile world.<div eID="gen37847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37848" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion--</hi>namely, Satan, the roaring, devouring lion (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.31">Lu 22:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.8">1Pe 5:8</reference>). I was prevented falling into his snare (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.26">2Ti 2:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.22.21">Psa 22:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.9">2Pe 2:9</reference>); <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.18">2Ti 4:18</reference> agrees with this interpretation, "The Lord shall deliver me from every evil work," namely, both from evil and the evil one, as the Greek of the Lord's Prayer expresses it. It was not deliverance from Nero (who was called the lion) which he rejoiced in, for he did not fear death (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.6-2Tim.4.8">2Ti 4:6-8</reference>), but deliverance from the temptation, through fear, to deny His Lord: so Alford. <div eID="gen37848" type="x-p"/>
entries.e7cc7320efc26b229e67fb13b9d841e5d150816a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18246"/><div sID="gen37849" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18246"/><hi type="bold">18. And the Lord shall, &c.--</hi>Hope draws its conclusions from the past to the future [Bengel].<div eID="gen37849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37850" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">will preserve me--</hi>literally, "will save" (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.21">Psa 22:21</reference>), "will bring me safe to." Jesus is the Lord and the Deliverer (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.20">Php 3:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.10">1Th 1:10</reference>): He saves from evil; He gives good things.<div eID="gen37850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37851" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heavenly kingdom--</hi>Greek, "His kingdom which is a heavenly one."<div eID="gen37851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37852" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to whom, &c.--</hi>Greek, "to whom be the glory unto the ages of ages." The very hope produces a doxology: how much greater will be the doxology which the actual enjoyment shall produce! [Bengel]. <div eID="gen37852" type="x-p"/>
entries.4ab17bd6f4d73702127b4aeaab09e04b97a8443f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18247"/><div sID="gen37853" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18247"/><hi type="bold">19. Prisca and Aquila--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Acts.18.2">Ac 18:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.18.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.16.3">Ro 16:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.16.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.19">1Co 16:19</reference>, written from Ephesus, where therefore Aquila and Priscilla must then have been).<div eID="gen37853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37854" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">household of Onesiphorus--</hi>If he were dead at the time, the "household" would not have been called "the household of Onesiphorus." He was probably absent (see on <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.16">2Ti 1:16</reference>). <div eID="gen37854" type="x-p"/>
entries.bdf95e39c6bb1fbf5f50bdb8793a42b853ec5fe6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18248"/><div sID="gen37855" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18248"/>20. In order to depict his desertion, he informs Timothy that Erastus, one of his usual companions (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.22">Ac 19:22</reference>, possibly the same Erastus as in <reference osisRef="Rom.16.23">Ro 16:23</reference>, though how he could leave his official duties for missionary journeys is not clear), stayed behind at Corinth, his native place, or usual residence, of which city he was "chamberlain," or city steward and treasurer (<reference osisRef="Rom.16.23">Ro 16:23</reference>); and Trophimus he left behind at Miletus sick. (On his former history, see on <reference osisRef="Acts.20.4">Ac 20:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.21.29">Ac 21:29</reference>). This verse is irreconcilable with the imprisonment from which he writes being the first: for he did not pass by Corinth or Miletus on his way to Rome when about to be imprisoned for the first time. As Miletus was near Ephesus, there is a presumption that Timothy was not at Ephesus when Paul wrote, or he would not need to inform Timothy of Trophimus lying sick in his immediate neighborhood. However, Trophimus may not have been still at Miletus at the time when Paul wrote, though he had left him there on his way to Rome. Prisca and Aquila were most likely to be at Ephesus (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.19">2Ti 4:19</reference>), and he desires Timothy to salute them: so also Onesiphorus' household (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.18">2Ti 1:18</reference>). Paul had not the power of healing at will (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.12">Ac 19:12</reference>), but as the Lord allowed him. <div eID="gen37855" type="x-p"/>
entries.32703f9b54ba71f1f642f27cefe0a291ad021572: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18249"/><div sID="gen37856" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18249"/><hi type="bold">21. before winter--</hi>when a voyage, according to ancient usages of navigation, would be out of the question: also, Paul would need his "cloak" against the winter (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.13">2Ti 4:13</reference>).<div eID="gen37856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37857" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Pudens ... Claudia--</hi>afterwards husband and wife (according to Martial [Epigrams, 4.13; 11.54]), he a Roman knight, she a Briton, surnamed Rufina. Tacitus [On Agriculture, 14], mentions that territories in southeast Britain were given to a British king; Cogidunus, in reward for his fidelity to Rome, A.D. 52, while Claudius was emperor. In 1772 a marble was dug up at Chichester, mentioning Cogidunus with the surname Claudius, added from his patron, the emperor's name; and Pudens in connection with Cogidunus, doubtless his father-in-law. His daughter would be Claudia, who seems to have been sent to Rome for education, as a pledge of the father's fidelity. Here she was under the protection of Pomponia, wife of Aulus Plautius, conqueror of Britain. Pomponia was accused of foreign superstitions, A.D. 57 [Tacitus, Annals, 3.32], probably Christianity. She probably was the instrument of converting Claudia, who took the name Rufina from her, that being a cognomen of the Pomponian gens (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.16.13">Ro 16:13</reference>, Rufus, a Christian). Pudens in Martial and in the Chichester inscription, appears as a pagan; but perhaps he or his friends concealed his Christianity through fear. Tradition represents Timothy, a son of Pudens, as taking part in converting the Britons.<div eID="gen37857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37858" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Linus--</hi>put third; therefore not at this time yet, as he was afterwards, bishop. His name being here inserted between Pudens and Claudia, implies the two were not yet married. "Eubulus" is identified by some with Aristobulus, who, with his converts, is said to have been among the first evangelists of Britain. Paul himself, says Clement, "visited the farthest west [perhaps Britain, certainly Spain], and was martyred under the rulers at Rome," who were Nero's vicegerents in his absence from the city. <div eID="gen37858" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a9ca6ea5fa4febd1c165a414103af462b76c99c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18250"/><div sID="gen37859" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18250"/><hi type="bold">22. Grace be with you--</hi>plural in oldest manuscripts, "with YOU," that is, thee and the members of the Ephesian and neighboring churches. <chapter eID="2Tim.4"/><div eID="gen37859" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen37524" osisID="2Tim" type="book"/>

entries.3924dc1ec71b8f640e5ed4b71bc8d8e5532f8ec8: <div eID="gen52147" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen52148" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen52149" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen52149" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen52148" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen52150" type="x-p"/> The apostle charges Timothy to be diligent, incessant, and faithful in his preaching; to watch, suffer patiently, and give full proof of his ministry, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.1-2Tim.4.5">2Tim 4:1-5</reference>. He predicts his own approaching death, and expresses the strongest confidence of being eternally happy, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.6-2Tim.4.8">2Tim 4:6-8</reference>. Desires Timothy to come and see him; shows that several had forsaken him, that others were gone to different districts, and that he had only Luke with him, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.9-2Tim.4.12">2Tim 4:9-12</reference>. Desires him to bring the cloak, book, and parchments, which he had left at Troas, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.13">2Tim 4:13</reference>. Of Alexander the coppersmith's opposition, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.14">2Tim 4:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.15">2Tim 4:15</reference>. Tells Timothy how he was deserted by all when obliged to make his first defense before Nero; how God supported him, and the confidence with which he was inspired, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.16-2Tim.4.18">2Tim 4:16-18</reference>. Salutations to different persons at Ephesus, and from different persons at Rome, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.19-2Tim.4.21">2Tim 4:19-21</reference>. The apostolical benediction, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.22">2Tim 4:22</reference>. <div eID="gen52150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52151" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen52151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52152" type="x-p"/> I charge thee therefore before God - Whose herald thou art; and before the Lord Jesus Christ, whose salvation thou art to proclaim, and who is coming to judge the world - all that shall be found then alive, and all that have died from the foundation of the world.
entries.b39bf82a7a3c59fdf36e5074a53ec4da59aac230: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen52152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52153" type="x-p"/> Preach the word - Κηρυξον τον λογον· Proclaim the doctrine, the doctrine of Christ crucified, for the sins of the whole world; the doctrine, that the Gentiles are invited to be fellow heirs with the Jews, and that for Jews and Gentiles there is no salvation but by faith in Christ. <div eID="gen52153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52154" type="x-p"/> Be instant in season, out of season - Επιστηθι ευκαιρως, ακαιρως. Be urgent whether the times be prosperous or adverse, whenever there is an opportunity; and when there is none, strive to make one. The Judge is at the door, and to every man eternity is at hand! Wherever thou meetest a sinner, speak to him the word of reconciliation. Do not be contented with stated times and accustomed places merely; all time and place belong to God, and are proper for his work. Wherever it can be done, there it should be done. Satan will omit neither time nor place where he can destroy. Omit thou none where thou mayest be the instrument of salvation to any. <div eID="gen52154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52155" type="x-p"/> Reprove - Ελεγξον· Confute, the false teacher. <div eID="gen52155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52156" type="x-p"/> Rebuke - Επιτιμησον· Reprove cuttingly and severely those who will not abandon their sins. <div eID="gen52156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52157" type="x-p"/> Exhort - Παρακαλεσον· Comfort the feeble-minded, the diffident and the tempted. <div eID="gen52157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52158" type="x-p"/> With all long-suffering - In reference to each and all of these cases. <div eID="gen52158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52159" type="x-p"/> And doctrine - The different modes of teaching suited to each.
entries.f0aeb091a318fc45bfa55b8d7266ca6f59a544ae: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen52159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52160" type="x-p"/> For the time will come - There is a time coming to the Church when men will not hear the practical truths of the Gospel, when they will prefer speculative opinions, which either do no good to the soul, or corrupt and destroy it, to that wholesome doctrine of "deny thyself, take up thy cross and follow me," which Jesus Christ has left in his Church. <div eID="gen52160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52161" type="x-p"/> But after their own lusts - For these they will follow, and hate those preachers and that doctrine by which they are opposed. <div eID="gen52161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52162" type="x-p"/> Shall they heap to themselves teachers - They will add one teacher to another, run and gad about after all, to find out those who insist not on the necessity of bearing the cross, of being crucified to the world, and of having the mind that was in Jesus. In this disposition interested men often find their account; they set up for teachers, "and widen and strew with flowers the way, down to eternal ruin," taking care to soothe the passions and flatter the vices of a trifling, superficial people. <div eID="gen52162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52163" type="x-p"/> Having itching ears - Endless curiosity, an insatiable desire of variety; and they get their ears tickled with the language and accent of the person, abandoning the good and faithful preacher for the fine speaker.
entries.bbdac6ab4daeb1a294007fb84c9b6f77c24ec101: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen52163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52164" type="x-p"/> And they shall turn away their ears from the truth - The truth strips them of their vices, sacrifices their idols, darts its lightnings against their easily besetting sins, and absolutely requires a conformity to a crucified Christ; therefore they turn their ears away from it. <div eID="gen52164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52165" type="x-p"/> And shall be turned unto fables - Believe any kind of stuff and nonsense; for, as one has justly observed, "Those who reject the truth are abandoned by the just judgment of God to credit the most degrading nonsense." This is remarkably the case with most deists; their creed often exhibits what is grossly absurd.
entries.f0d52c3b18e2910e73db43ce3f5ebf69c62dc886: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen52165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52166" type="x-p"/> But watch thou in all things - It is possible to be overtaken in a fault, to neglect one's duty, and to lose one's soul. Watching unto prayer prevents all these evils. <div eID="gen52166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52167" type="x-p"/> Endure afflictions - Let no sufferings affright thee; nor let the dread of them either cause thee to abandon the truth, or relax in thy zeal for the salvation of men. <div eID="gen52167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52168" type="x-p"/> Do the work of an evangelist - That is: Preach Christ crucified for the sins of the whole world; for this, and this alone, is doing the work of an evangelist, or preacher of the glad tidings of peace and salvation by Christ. An angel from God was first sent to do the work of an evangelist, and how did he do it? Behold, said he, I bring you good tidings of great joy; Ιδου γαρ, ευαγγελιζομαι ὑμιν χαραν μεγαλην, ἡτις εσται παντι τῳ λαῳ. Behold, I evangelize unto you great joy, which shall be to all people; to you is born a Savior. Those who do not proclaim Christ as having tasted death for every man, and who do not implicitly show that every human soul may be saved, do not perform the work of evangelists; they, God help them! limit the Holy One of Israel. Yet, as far as they preach the truth in sincerity, so far God acknowledges and blesses them and their labors; they do a part of the work, but not the whole. <div eID="gen52168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52169" type="x-p"/> Make full proof of thy ministry - Push all thy principles to their utmost power of activity; carry them on to all their consequences; and try what God will do for thee, and by thee. Neglect no part of thy sacred function; perform faithfully all the duties of which it is composed; and do God's work in his own way and in his own spirit.
entries.5f067321834ff1ecb3472ddffed1f9cbd4dc2fec: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen52169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52170" type="x-p"/> For I am now ready to be offered - Ηδη σπενδομαι· I am already poured out as a libation. See the note on <reference osisRef="Phi.2.17">Phi 2:17</reference>. He considers himself as on the eve of being sacrificed, and looks upon his blood as the libation which was poured on the sacrificial offering. He could not have spoken thus positively had not the sentence of death been already passed upon him.
entries.53c6b3e98693142638c59979996dc44bf030d5f1: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen52170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52171" type="x-p"/> I have fought a good fight - Every reader will perceive that the apostle, as was his very frequent custom, alludes to the contests at the Grecian games: Τον αγυνα τον καλον ηγωνισμαι· I have wrestled that good wrestling - I have struggled hard, and have over come, in a most honorable cause. <div eID="gen52171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52172" type="x-p"/> I have finished my course - I have started for the prize, and have come up to the goal, outstripping all my competitors, and have gained this prize also. <div eID="gen52172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen52173" type="x-p"/> I have kept the faith - As the laws of these games must be most diligently observed and kept, (for though a man overcome, yet is he not crowned, except he strive lawfully), so I have kept the rules of the spiritual combat and race; and thus, having contended lawfully, and conquered in each exercise, I have a right to expect the prize.
